The Story of Chilat-Putra

I bow to Lord Jina, whose bright eye is omniscience, and I write the story of Chilat-Putra.

King Upshrenik of Rajgriha once went outside the city for a breath of fresh air. The horse he rode was very unruly and carried him into a fearsome forest. The forest belonged to a hunter named Yamdand. He had a daughter named Tilakvati, who was very beautiful. Seeing her, Upshrenik was pierced by the arrows of desire. Seeing his condition, Yamdand said to him, "O king of kings, if you agree to make the son born of her the master of your kingdom, I can marry her to you." Upshrenik accepted Yamdand's conditions, and Yamdand married Tilakvati to him. Pleased, Upshrenik took her back to Rajgriha.

For many days, he enjoyed happiness with Tilakvati. A son was born to her, named Chilat-Putra. Upshrenik had other sons from his first queens. Although he had pledged to give the kingdom to Tilakvati's son, he always worried that the kingdom might fall into ruin under his rule. Yet he was bound by his promise.

One day, he summoned a learned astrologer and asked, "Pandit, using your knowledge of omens, tell me — which of my sons will be fit to rule?" The astrologer thought deeply and replied, "Maharaj, I shall explain. Let all your sons sit together to eat kheer, and then release a pack of dogs upon them. The one who, fearless, remains seated on the throne, beats the drum, eats his food, and feeds the dogs from afar — he has the quality of a king. That is, through his wisdom, he should keep the dogs away by touch while eating. The second test is this: when a fire breaks out, the one who can rescue the throne, umbrella, chowries, and other royal symbols will be fit to be king."

After some days, Upshrenik arranged to test his sons according to the astrologer's instructions. When the dogs were released, all the other sons ran away in fear — except Chilat-Putra. He sat calmly on the throne, beat the drum, ate his kheer, and fed the dogs from a distance, keeping them away without touching them. In the fire test too, he alone rescued the royal symbols.

Through these tests, Chilat-Putra proved himself the most worthy. Upshrenik made him the crown prince, and in time, Chilat-Putra became king. He ruled with justice and compassion, following the path of dharma. He worshipped Lord Jina daily, gave generously to the worthy, and protected his subjects with care.

One day, a great monk came to his city and delivered a discourse on the impermanence of worldly life. Chilat-Putra's heart was transformed. He realised that despite all his power and wisdom, he was still subject to birth, death, and suffering. He renounced his kingdom, took initiation as a monk, and practised intense austerities. Through dedicated spiritual practice, he destroyed his karmas and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that true worthiness to rule is not determined by birth or seniority but by courage, wisdom, and composure under pressure. Chilat-Putra, though born of a hunter's daughter, proved himself the most worthy through his fearlessness and intelligence. The wise should cultivate these qualities and use their positions of power for the welfare of all beings.
